surface: rightsplit — microsite /apps/rightsplit/ (Persuade) + /apps/rightsplit/privacy/, /apps/rightsplit/support/ and the alternatives pages that target it: /alternatives/splitwise/, /alternatives/tricount/, /alternatives/settle-up/, /alternatives/tab/, /alternatives/venmo-split/ (Read variants)

dossier.mechanism: One phone photographs the receipt and Apple's on-device Vision reads every line. The holder taps each line onto whoever ordered it and splits shared plates only among the people who shared them. RightSplit then spreads tax and tip in proportion to each person's subtotal, applies a fair-rounding pass, and sends each person only their own total over iMessage or WhatsApp. Nobody else installs anything, there is no account, and the receipt image never leaves the phone.
dossier.audienceScene: The end of a dinner, bar night or group trip: 2–12 people, one check, mixed orders (the $14 salad beside the $48 steak), someone reaching for a napkin. The visitor arrives on an iPhone from Google or an AI answer ('bill splitter app', 'split bill by item', 'Splitwise alternative'). Sometimes they are still at the table; more often it is the morning after an even split cost them $20. On desktop they are planning a trip or weighing RightSplit against Splitwise or Tab, and the app has to reach the phone by QR. The audience spans the US and Europe: the app's own screenshots show $92.39 and €65.85, and the UI ships in 32 languages.
dossier.culturalHome: The end-of-meal ritual, not fintech: the thermal check from the POS printer, the folder it arrives in with cards fanned out of its top, the initials and circles people pen onto the check, napkin math, 'separate checks?', the pencil tally on a pub beer coaster, the conveyor-sushi plate stack counted at your seat, and the shop-counter label that charges every customer the same rate per kilo.
dossier.mustProve: In the first viewport: (1) one real-looking bill turning into different per-person totals with tip spread in proportion. This uses the journal's worked example, labelled illustrative: on a $154.65 check the $58 ribeye pays $74.75 and the $14 salad pays $18.04, against $38.66 each split evenly. (2) The promise 'scan, split, send — only you need the app, no account, the receipt never leaves the phone'. (3) The honest price line from price.value: 'Free — Pro from $3.99/yr or $7.99 lifetime'. (4) The working official App Store badge, plus the QR on desktop.
dossier.categoryDefault: Blue fintech friendliness: white-to-blue gradient, rounded sans, split hero with a phone mockup, cartoon friends or circled avatars, a pie chart, 'Split bills with friends easily', teal-green money accents (Splitwise), a row of feature cards and star testimonials. RightSplit's own icon, a white pie with one slice pulled out on a blue gradient squircle, already sits in this rut.
dossier.predictableOpposite: The cream bistro menu: warm paper, serif display, chalkboard or terracotta accents (the incumbent Paper & Ink and the AI default). Or the app UI blown up to page size: a navy-to-maroon gradient dashboard of totals with neon cyan.
dossier.literalReading: 'RightSplit' read literally is the correct cut: a pie or cake divided into fair slices, which is exactly the app icon. Only candidate 7 uses it.

Journal 'The bill-splitting math nobody agrees on'. Worked example: $120 subtotal, 8.875% NYC tax $10.65, 20% tip $24.00, total $154.65. Dana ribeye $58 → $74.75, Ben pasta and beer $28 → $36.09, Cara burger $20 → $25.78, Alex salad $14 → $18.04; even split $38.66. Design reasoning: 'move the itemising off the table... People do not object to receiving a total. They object to watching one get constructed about them.'
Journal 'How to split a Valentine's dinner without making it weird': a $312 table of four (three steaks, one salad). It claims payment deeplinks that the app FAQ denies (content drift).

candidates.name: The thermal restaurant check, torn into one receipt per person
candidates.why: The one object in every diner's hand at the end of every meal, and the thing RightSplit actually scans. It carries the mechanism as one printed roll whose lines get circled in ballpoint to assign them, then torn into four short receipts, each ending in its own TOTAL: scan, split, send, in paper.

candidates.name: The table from above: seat positions and the reach zone
candidates.family: cartography/diagram — the server's seat-position plan and the etiquette-book place-setting diagram
candidates.why: Servers track who ordered what by seat number, and every diner remembers who sat where and who reached for the bread. It carries the mechanism by placing each line at the seat that ordered it, shared plates in the reach zone between the people who had them (the journal's 'everyone who could reach it' rule), the bottle between the drinkers, and each seat's total printed at its edge.

candidates.name: Conveyor-sushi plate stacks and the plate-colour price chart
candidates.family: ritual/place — a restaurant's pricing system (melamine plates, conveyor, price key)
candidates.why: The purest item-level settlement diners know: you pay for exactly the plates stacked at your seat, and nobody argues. It carries the mechanism by turning receipt lines into plates coming round the belt, each taken onto a person's stack and counted into that person's total.

candidates.name: The check presenter with cards fanned out of its top
candidates.family: ritual object — leatherette folder, foil stamp, card slot
candidates.why: The folder arrives once and goes back once, and the moment four cards stick out of it is exactly when 'just split it four ways' happens. It carries the mechanism by standing each person's own amount up out of the folder's top edge instead of four identical charges, with the badge in the card slot.

candidates.name: The beer-coaster tally (Bierdeckel strokes)
candidates.family: bar print ephemera — cardboard coaster, pencil tally
candidates.why: In German and Austrian bars your own coaster is your tab, marked with a stroke per drink and settled coaster by coaster: per-person splitting with no account. It carries the mechanism with one coaster per diner and a stroke per item, shared rounds marked across several coasters, and each coaster settling to its own number.

candidates.name: The deli-scale price label
candidates.family: instrument/measurement — price-computing scale label, EU unit price
candidates.why: Everyone has read one: net weight times the same price per kilo equals your price. It carries the proportional rule exactly: each diner's items are the 'weight', the table's tax-plus-tip rate is the 'unit price', identical on every label, and the total is the printed price.

candidates.name: The pie, cut by what each person ate (literal reading)
candidates.why: The icon's own pie, recut so each slice is sized by what that person ordered instead of equal wedges. It carries proportional shares directly, but it is the name and icon read literally and sits beside the category's pie-chart rut.

styles.label: Weighed and Priced
styles.lineage: Labels printed by price-computing deli and butcher-counter scales (Bizerba, Mettler Toledo, DIGI, Avery Berkel) under the EU unit-price rule (Directive 98/6/EC), which puts a price per kilo beside every total. They are die-cut self-adhesive labels issued one after another on a backing liner. Each has pre-printed spot-colour boxes overprinted in thermal black, small caps field captions (NET WT · PRICE/kg · PRICE), the total in heavy numerals, packed-on and use-by dates, and an EAN-13 with the price embedded (GS1 prefixes 20–29).
styles.thesis: A fair split is one rate applied to different weights. The page prints each diner a deli price label: their items are the net weight, the table's tax-plus-tip rate is the unit price (pre-printed cyan and identical on every label), and their total is the price. It refuses the blue-fintech split hero, the avatar pie and the equal-wedge diagram.
styles.scene: A shopper reads a label at the counter under flat white shop light, or on a phone in daylight. Everything is printed, matte and bright, so the scheme is light only (color-scheme: light).

palette.role: Process cyan: the backing liner (page ground between labels, 40–55% of every viewport) and the pre-printed RATE box on every label. It is the system's constant. Black on it is 7.4:1; never white text on it.
Label stock: every die-cut label (each section), the sticky label, the badge and QR fields
Thermal black: all type, 1px field frames, 2px price-box frames, barcodes, registration marks on the liner, 3px focus ring (18.6:1 on white)
Small-print grey: field sub-lines, footnotes, the even-split comparison line, ingredient small print (6.1:1 on white)
Counter red: only the 'Not assigned' row and the over/under-collected warning in the interactive scale (6.9:1 on white)

styles.navigation: A thin header label at the top of the roll: 'RightSplit' (back to top) and five plain links — The labels, How it weighs, Price, Questions, Privacy — with a 2px black underline on the current section. On phones, 'Menu' opens a full-width white label listing the same links as captioned rows. In-page anchors only; the Lagerland strip at the foot is the only way out.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'Reprint the labels'. One label holds the sample receipt (Ribeye 58.00, Pasta, beer 28.00, Burger 20.00, Salad 14.00; tagged illustrative) with a person select on each line, a tax field (8.875%) and a tip stepper (0–25%). Any change reprints the four diner labels. The cyan RATE box takes the same new value on every label. NET and PRICE recalculate using the plateau_disclosure rule (proportional tax and tip, fair-rounding pass), and each EAN-13 is redrawn for the new price. An aria-live='polite' line reads, for example, 'Rate is now × 1.30875 for everyone. Alex pays $18.32.' An unassigned line adds a red 'Not assigned: $20.00' row, the app's own state. No JS: the four labels are server-rendered with the worked-example values and the controls are left out. Reduced motion: labels change in place.
styles.motionGrammar: Printed and still. Under html.js only: each label enters by sliding 8px down out of an implied printer slot while fading 0→1 over 140ms (40ms stagger, first reveal only); reprinted labels repeat the same slide; the RATE value crossfades over 100ms; the sticky label rises in 160ms ease-out. No parallax, no count-ups (every price is server-rendered), no hover lifts. prefers-reduced-motion turns all of it off.
styles.readModeVariant: The same roll, quieter. The cyan liner becomes a 24px frame and the gaps; the reading column is one long white label at 68ch, Pathway Extreme 400 (wdth 100) at 18px/1.6. The black band names the page ('PRIVACY POLICY · RIGHTSPLIT', 'SUPPORT · RIGHTSPLIT', 'SPLITWISE ALTERNATIVE'). The H1 sits in the PRODUCT field at 56px (wdth 75, wght 860), and the quick answer is the WHAT IT IS field. Privacy sections become captioned fields (OVERVIEW, DATA COLLECTION, STORAGE, THIRD PARTIES, CHILDREN, CHANGES, CONTACT), with transparency.yml as a FREE FROM line. Support is a contact label with the email and 'what to include' as captioned fields, faq rows below. Alternatives pages set RightSplit and the competitor as two side-by-side labels with the same captions (Workflow, Item-level, Account, Ongoing balances). RightSplit's column carries the cyan pre-print; pick-if lists and a GET IT field close the page.
styles.assetsNeeded: None new: icon, 4 screenshots, assets/qr/rightsplit.svg. EAN-13 barcodes are inline SVG computed from each price (hand-built for the four static labels, regenerated by JS in the interaction).
styles.risk: The metaphor needs one sentence to land (dinner is not sold by the kilo), so the RATE caption must say 'tax + tip ÷ subtotal, the same for everyone' wherever it appears. At a glance, a cyan-and-white page can be mistaken for blue fintech; only the label grammar (black band, captions, heavy prices, barcodes) prevents that. The demo maths must match the app's fair-rounding exactly: rounded naively, the worked example sums to $154.66 against a $154.65 receipt.
styles.memoryTest: The cyan page of white price labels: every diner's label had the same cyan '× 1.28875' box and a different price. The salad paid $18.04, the ribeye $74.75.

styles.label: Torn Per Person
styles.lineage: The 80 mm thermal restaurant check from an Epson TM-T88-class POS printer: merchant header in double-width capitals, a SERVER / TABLE / GUESTS line, item lines with right-aligned prices and dotted leaders, the suggested-gratuity block US checks print, and the sawtooth edge from the printer's tear bar. At the table it gets marked up with a four-colour ballpoint (Bic 4 Colours, 1970): circled lines, ticks and initials in blue, red, green and black, the way people split a check by hand.
styles.thesis: The page is the check itself: one thermal roll running down the screen, its lines circled in four ballpoint inks to show who ordered what, then torn into one short receipt per person, each ending in its own TOTAL. The bill is the interface. It refuses the fintech phone-mockup hero and the avatar pie.
styles.scene: The check has just landed on the table and someone is reading it on a phone in a bright room. The page is the paper, matte and cool white, with ink on it, so the scheme is light only (color-scheme: light).

type.display: Azeret Mono 700 (latin ≈10.6 KB) for printed headers. The H1 is 'double-height' at 52px desktop / 30px mobile, uppercase via CSS so the source text stays as written. The wordmark, section headers and every TOTAL line are 'double-width' (transform: scaleX(2) on short single lines; wrapping is computable from the fixed 0.6em advance).
type.text: Golos Text 400 and 600 (≈12 KB each) for all reading prose (subheadline, how-it-works detail, plateau rule, FAQ answers, privacy) at 18px/1.6 in a 64ch column. Azeret Mono 400 for receipt lines and amounts at 17px, with tnum.
type.utility: Nanum Pen Script 400 (≈15 KB) for ballpoint initials, names and margin notes only, at 24px or larger. Never body text, and every handwritten name is also printed.
type.rationale: Receipt lines are fixed-pitch data, so a monospace is honest here, not a costume. Azeret Mono's squared grotesk forms sit close to a POS printer's built-in font, and it has nine weights and tnum. Golos Text is a plain, open screen grotesk, so the explanation reads as prose rather than more receipt. Nanum Pen Script is a quick ballpoint hand and the only face that is written rather than printed. ≈60 KB in all.

styles.navigation: The receipt's header line is the nav: 'RIGHTSPLIT' (top) and five plain links — The check, Tear it, Price, Questions, Privacy — in Azeret 400 with a dotted underline that becomes a solid ballpoint-blue underline on hover and focus. styles.signatureInteraction: 'Tear it'. Under the check sits a printed line, '- - TEAR ALONG THE INK - -', that works as a button. Pressing it pulls the check apart into four narrow receipts: four across at ≥1024px, two by two on mobile. Each receipt is headed by the person's initial in their ink and lists their lines, TAX SHARE, TIP SHARE and a double-width TOTAL (Dana 74.75, Ben 36.09, Cara 25.78, Alex 18.04). A fifth strip in faded grey reads 'SPLIT EVENLY: 38.66 EACH'. Before tearing, tapping a line on the check moves it to the next person's ink, and the torn totals recompute with the plateau_disclosure rule. aria-live announces 'Alex: 18.04'. No JS: the four torn receipts are server-rendered under the check with the worked-example values, and the button is absent. Reduced motion: the torn receipts appear in place without separating.
styles.motionGrammar: Paper does not glide. Under html.js only: ink circles draw on once (SVG stroke-dashoffset, 320ms each, 80ms apart) when the check enters view; the tear moves the pieces 12px apart in 180ms ease-out; the sticky slip rises in 160ms. No scroll-jacking, no count-ups. prefers-reduced-motion: ink starts fully drawn, tears are static, nothing moves.
styles.readModeVariant: One long receipt at 68ch. Privacy, support and alternatives pages print as a single roll: a double-width header ('PRIVACY POLICY — RIGHTSPLIT'), the quick answer as the message block between '* * *', headings in Azeret 700, reading text in Golos 400 at 18px/1.6. Sections are divided by dotted rules, not tears (tears belong to the app page's per-person split). Ink appears only as the blue link underline and one margin note per page. Alternatives pages set two receipts side by side, 'RIGHTSPLIT' and the competitor, with matching lines (Workflow, Item-level, Account, Ongoing balances), then 'Pick RightSplit if' ticked green and 'Stick with Splitwise if' in black. Support prints the contact block as a receipt with the email on the TOTAL line.
styles.assetsNeeded: None new: ink marks are inline SVG paths, the check is set type, and the screenshots, icon and QR exist.
styles.risk: Familiar: the page-as-receipt is the obvious creative answer for a bill app, and receipt-styled pages are a known web trope (receipt generators, playlist receipts). Its strength has to come from the ink assignment and the tear, not the paper. Long lines of mono tire the eye, so prose must stay in Golos. Handwritten initials must stay legible at 24px and never carry meaning alone.
styles.memoryTest: A long white receipt with its lines circled in blue, red and green pen that tore into four little receipts, one per person, each with its own total.

styles.label: Cards in the Folder
styles.lineage: The restaurant check presenter: a padded leatherette book-fold, about 24 × 12 cm closed, with stitched edges, a clear vinyl pocket for the check, a card slot, a small card pocket and a pen loop, and the house name foil-stamped on the cover. It ends every group meal the same way: each diner slides a card into its top edge, so the folder goes back with the cards fanned out above it and the server asks 'split it evenly?'
styles.thesis: A meal ends in a folder that arrives once and goes back once. The page is that folder opened on the table, with each person's own amount standing up out of its top edge where the cards go, so the visitor sees four different numbers come back instead of one total cut four ways. It refuses the split hero and the avatar pie by making the folder's two leaves, its pockets and its top edge the page's structure.
styles.scene: A dim dining room late in the evening. The folder lies open on a dark table in front of whoever picked it up; the light is low, the leather matte, and the only bright things are the foil, the cards and one paper card. The scheme is dark only (color-scheme: dark).

type.display: Funnel Display 600 and 800 (latin ≈10.7 KB each), always as foil. H1 at 80px desktop / 46px mobile (800); section titles at 40/30px (600); card amounts at 40px desktop / 22px mobile (800, tnum).
type.text: Onest 400 and 500 (≈15 KB each): reading text in white foil on leather at 18px/1.65, captions at 15px in thread colour, nav at 16px (500); tnum on amounts.
type.rationale: Hot-foil stamping fills in fine joins. Funnel Display's notched joins (visible in n, k and a at display sizes) look like a die cut to survive that, and it stays crisp at 80px on dark leather without the gold-script steakhouse cliché. Onest has open apertures and a generous x-height, which hold up as light text on a dark ground. ≈52 KB in all.

styles.signatureInteraction: 'Split it evenly?' A foil-stamped two-way switch (a real radio group) sits beside the cards: 'By what each ordered' (default) or 'Evenly'. Choosing Evenly lowers or raises all four cards to the same height and changes them to $38.66, and each card gains a thread-colour line with its difference: Alex '+$20.62', Dana '−$36.09'. Switching back restores the RightSplit amounts. aria-live reads 'Evenly: everyone pays $38.66. Alex pays $20.62 more than by item.' No JS: the cards render at by-item heights, with a printed line underneath: 'Split evenly it would be $38.66 each — Alex would pay $20.62 more than the salad cost.' The switch is hidden. Reduced motion: heights and amounts change instantly.
styles.motionGrammar: Leather does not move; cards do. Under html.js only: the four cards slide up out of the pocket on first reveal (translateY 40px→0, 240ms ease-out, 60ms stagger); the switch changes card heights over 200ms ease-in-out; the sticky strip rises in 180ms. No parallax, no glows, no count-ups. prefers-reduced-motion: cards are already standing, heights change instantly.

Privacy, support and alternatives pages show a single oxblood leaf with stitched edges and a foil-stamped title ('Privacy policy', 'Support', 'RightSplit vs Splitwise'). The reading column is the paper card held in the clear pocket: foil-white #F3E8EA ground, table-ink text, Onest 400 at 18px/1.65, 66ch, headings in Funnel 600. styles.assetsNeeded: None new: grain and stitching are CSS and inline SVG, and the cards are set type. Optional later: Apple's official white 'Download on the App Store' badge artwork, if the owner wants the badge directly on leather instead of on a foil-white tab.
styles.risk: Dark, warm leather sits near the steakhouse rendition, so it must stay off gold, scripts and serifs. The folder must remain one folder: two leaves on desktop and one on mobile, with no extra flaps. Its sections below the hero are stitched compartments of the same leather, so the object reading can thin into 'dark page with dashed borders' if the stitching is not drawn with care. Card shapes could imply that RightSplit takes payment, which it does not, so the copy must say 'RightSplit does the math; everyone pays their own way'. Light-on-dark reading needs the paper card for long text.
styles.memoryTest: The burgundy leather check folder with four coloured cards sticking out of the top, each a different height and amount, until you pressed 'Evenly' and they all sank to $38.66.

canon: Canon (standing exit, never recommended): the blue fintech bill-splitter page played straight. Blue-to-white gradient hero, 'Split bills with friends, fairly' beside an iPhone mockup of the item-assignment screen, App Store badge with QR, three icon cards (Scan · Split · Send), Free / Pro / Lifetime pricing table with Lifetime highlighted, a Splitwise comparison grid and a FAQ accordion, all in a rounded geometric sans with light and dark themes.
notes: Roll ran degraded: the roll service was unreachable, so there were no catalog challengers and no quality-bar boards. Seed 844f72bb assigned candidate 6; re-roll 1 gave 4, which was distinct, so no further re-rolls were needed. The seven candidates were ordered by resonance before the roll. Neither roll hit candidate 1, so it appears as IMPECCABLE’S PICK (B). App truth: freemium, 'Free — Pro from $3.99/yr or $7.99 lifetime' (schema 0 / 7.99 / 3 offers), iOS only, live, ratings 5.0 from 1 (no stars anywhere). Content drift the build must not copy: alternatives/tab.html prices Pro at $1.99/year; alternatives/splitwise.html says item-by-item is the default (front matter makes it Pro); the Valentine's journal post promises Venmo/PayPal/iMessage Cash deeplinks and drag-to-assign, which the app FAQ contradicts ('Not directly'); the privacy policy names Contacts and Photos, while transparency.yml lists Camera only. All three directions use the journal's worked example ($154.65 → 74.75 / 36.09 / 25.78 / 18.04; even split 38.66), labelled illustrative. Rounded naively it sums to $154.66, so the interactive demos must implement plateau_disclosure's fair-rounding pass and be checked against the app before shipping. 'Most chosen' on the lifetime plan is front-matter copy (plans[2].summary); render it only as written. training_vocabulary.overline ('Speaks the language') is an eyebrow and is dropped per the craft floor. The markdown body exists but show_body is not set. Faces verified on Fontsource with fontTools (all have tnum): Pathway Extreme (wdth 75–100, wght 100–900), Azeret Mono, Golos Text, Nanum Pen Script, Funnel Display (300–800), Onest. Font budgets: A ≈58 KB, B ≈60 KB, C ≈52 KB, none shared with the sibling boards written so far. No founder, spotlight, roadmap, insight gallery or creative_work blocks exist, so none are drawn.
